opus-5.5.text:
I think a couple of years ago the field was really split. One camp said simulation and synthetic data would be the main path, since real-robot data is slow and expensive to collect, so you should build great simulators, generate massive data, and do sim-to-real transfer. The other camp said the sim-to-real gap is too large, especially for contact-rich manipulation, and that the only thing that really works is real-world data, from teleoperation and from deployed robots.

What I see now is that these views are converging toward a more pragmatic middle. Most serious teams agree that real-world data is the anchor. It defines the distribution you care about, and nothing fully replaces the physics of real contact, deformable objects, friction, and sensor noise. But almost nobody thinks real data alone will scale fast enough. So synthetic data becomes a multiplier, not a substitute.

Where people now agree it clearly works is locomotion and whole-body control. Reinforcement learning in simulation with heavy domain randomization has basically won there, and that's why you see humanoids walking, running, and doing flips. For dexterous manipulation it's more nuanced. Simulation helps a lot with pretraining, data augmentation, rendering new viewpoints, lighting, and textures, and generating long-tail scenarios. But the final policy quality still comes from real interaction data.

The other big shift is what "synthetic" even means. It's no longer just physics engines. People increasingly use video generation models and world models to synthesize training data, or learn from large amounts of human video and then retarget. So the debate has moved from "sim versus real" to "what's the right data pyramid?" At the base, huge amounts of cheap data like internet video and synthetic generation. In the middle, human demonstration data. At the top, a smaller but very high-quality layer of real robot data. I think most companies are now roughly aligned on that structure. The differences are really about proportions, and about which layer each team believes will deliver the next breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response describes earlier disagreement and current convergence, but does not say companies publicly reject synthetic data while privately using synthetic-data services.

r002.rationale: It calls synthetic data a multiplier and says it can help with pretraining and augmentation, but does not claim that co-training synthetic and real data improves deployed model performance.

r003.rationale: The response describes broad agreement on a data pyramid and differences in proportions, but does not distinguish a mature rationale for synthetic data from immature specific algorithms or data approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the convergence has been pretty striking, honestly. Two years ago you could put ten embodied-intelligence founders in a room and get ten different answers about synthetic data. Some people were saying simulation is the whole game, some were saying nothing counts except real robot hours, and a lot of people were somewhere in the middle without a clear position. Now the positions have narrowed a lot.

The first thing people agree on is that pure real-world data doesn't scale on its own. Teleoperation is expensive, it's slow, and the diversity you get is limited by how many operators and how many setups you can afford. Everyone has run into that wall. So even the companies that started out as "real data purists" have accepted that they need some synthetic layer, whether that's simulation, generative video models, or augmentation of real trajectories.

The second thing people agree on, and this one came from the other direction, is that synthetic data alone doesn't close the loop. The sim-to-real gap is still real. Contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, friction, all of that is hard to model well. So the simulation-first camps have had to admit they need a real-data anchor to calibrate against.

So where everyone is landing is some version of a pyramid. A relatively small amount of high-quality real data at the top that defines what "correct" looks like, a much larger volume of synthetic data in the middle for coverage and diversity, and then internet-scale video and language data at the base for priors. The debates now are about ratios and about which layer deserves the next dollar, not about whether the layers exist.

The other interesting shift is how people think about what synthetic data is for. Early on it was treated as a substitute for real data. Now most teams treat it as a tool for specific jobs: covering long-tail failure cases, testing robustness, generating variations of scenes you've already seen in the real world. That's a more mature view. You're not asking the simulator to replace reality, you're asking it to multiply the value of the reality you already collected.

Where I still see real disagreement is on generative world models. Some companies believe that a video model that can predict physically plausible futures will eventually become the primary synthetic data engine and make hand-built simulators obsolete. Others think those models are great for visual diversity but hallucinate physics in ways that are dangerous for control. I don't think that debate is settled, and I think the answer may depend on which tasks you care about.

But the overall direction is clear. The question has moved from "synthetic or real" to "how do we build a data flywheel where each type makes the other more useful." That's a healthier place for the industry to be.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that companies publicly reject synthetic data while privately using synthetic-data services.

r002.rationale: It describes combining real and synthetic data as a data flywheel, but does not claim that co-training on them improves deployed model performance.

r003.rationale: It presents the broad case for synthetic data as settled and mature, while describing disagreement and unresolved questions about particular approaches such as generative world models.

astra-6.text:
I think the views are converging around a practical question: does synthetic data improve what the robot can actually do? It’s less about choosing between synthetic and real data, and more about understanding which role each should play.

Real-world data grounds the system in actual interactions. Synthetic data can expand coverage, vary conditions, and give you examples that would be expensive or difficult to collect. But generating more data isn’t automatically useful. You still have to test whether the resulting model performs better in the real world.

So I’d expect convergence around a loop: collect real data, identify where the model fails, generate targeted synthetic examples, and validate on the robot. Companies may still disagree about the mix, but the standard for judging it becomes the same: how much useful capability transfers.

r001.rationale: It discusses choosing roles for synthetic and real data, but says nothing about companies publicly rejecting synthetic data while privately using its services.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic data should be validated for real-world improvement, but does not claim that co-training on synthetic and real data improves deployed model performance.

r003.rationale: It describes possible uses and validation of synthetic data, but does not distinguish a mature broad rationale from immature specific algorithms and data approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the views are converging around a practical point: synthetic data is necessary, but its value depends on whether it improves performance in the real world. The question is shifting from “Should we use synthetic data?” to “What should we synthesize, and how do we validate it?”

Real-world data helps you discover where the model fails. Synthetic data lets you expand those situations, vary the conditions, and train at a scale that would be expensive to collect physically. Then you have to put the model back on the robot and see whether those improvements transfer.

So I expect convergence around a loop: collect real data, identify failures, generate targeted synthetic data, and validate in the real world. Companies may still disagree about the mix, but the useful measure is how much reliable capability that loop produces.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention companies publicly rejecting synthetic data while privately using synthetic-data services.

r002.rationale: It describes using real data to identify failures and synthetic data to expand training, then checking transfer, but does not claim that co-training on both improves deployed performance.
